title: Buffering, Caching & Spooling
summary: How the OS smooths speed mismatches between devices and the CPU — buffering, the page cache, and why a successful write() doesn't mean your data is safe on disk.

slides.markdown:
Devices and the CPU operate at wildly different speeds — a CPU can execute billions of instructions per second while a disk delivers data in milliseconds and a network link's throughput varies unpredictably. **Buffering** and **caching** absorb that mismatch so neither side has to wait lockstep for the other.

This topic covers the mechanics (single, double, and circular buffering), the specific case of the OS's disk/page cache, and one of the most consequential gaps in this whole area for interviews: the difference between "my write() returned" and "my data is actually durable."

slides.sectionTitle: Why I/O needs buffering: speed mismatch
slides.markdown:
A **buffer** is a memory region that temporarily holds data in transit between a producer and a consumer running at different rates. Without one, a fast producer (the CPU generating data to write) would have to stall waiting for a slow consumer (a disk or network link) to catch up on every single unit of data — or vice versa, a fast device would have to wait on a slow CPU to process each chunk it delivers.

Buffering decouples the two: the producer can get ahead by filling the buffer, and the consumer drains it at its own pace, as long as the buffer doesn't run empty (starving the consumer) or fill up entirely (blocking the producer).

**Single buffering** uses one buffer: the producer fills it, then the consumer drains it, strictly alternating — while either side is actively using the buffer, the other must wait its turn. It's simple but leaves the pipeline idle roughly half the time.

**Double buffering** uses two buffers: while the consumer drains buffer A, the producer is already filling buffer B; when both finish, they swap roles. This overlaps production and consumption almost entirely — the classic example is video rendering, where the GPU draws the next frame into an off-screen buffer while the display shows the previous, already-complete frame, avoiding visible tearing or a stall.

slides.markdown:
![double buffering overlapping fill and drain](assets/double-buffering-overlap.svg)

The offset is the entire mechanism: at any instant, one buffer is being filled while the other is being drained, so neither the producer nor the consumer ever idles waiting for a single shared buffer to free up.

Compare this to single buffering, where the equivalent diagram would show one bar with fill and drain segments strictly alternating — visible idle gaps wherever the other side has to wait its turn.

assets.alt: double buffering overlapping fill and drain

slides.markdown:
A **circular (ring) buffer** generalizes double buffering to N slots arranged in a logical circle, with a write pointer and a read pointer chasing each other around it. The producer writes at the write pointer and advances it; the consumer reads at the read pointer and advances it; as long as the write pointer never laps the read pointer (buffer full) and the read pointer never laps the write pointer (buffer empty), both sides proceed independently.

This is the standard structure for continuous streaming I/O — audio buffers, network packet rings (NIC receive/transmit rings are literally circular buffers in hardware), and pipe implementations — because it needs no buffer-swapping logic, just pointer arithmetic, and scales naturally to bursty producers or consumers without needing a fixed two-buffer handoff.

slides.sectionTitle: The disk/page cache: buffering reads and writes in memory
slides.markdown:
The kernel keeps a **page cache** (Linux terminology; similar concept elsewhere) — recently read or written disk blocks held in otherwise-unused RAM. A `read()` first checks the page cache; a hit returns data at memory speed with zero disk I/O, while a miss triggers an actual disk read that also populates the cache for next time. A `write()` similarly lands in the page cache first (marking those pages **dirty**) and is flushed to disk later, asynchronously.

This is why repeatedly reading the same file is dramatically faster the second time, and why `free -h` on Linux shows most "free" RAM actually allocated to cache — the kernel deliberately uses otherwise-idle memory for this, reclaiming it instantly if an application needs it.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: write-back vs write-through caching policies
slides.markdown:
| | Write-back | Write-through |
|---|---|---|
| When disk is updated | Later, asynchronously (write marks page dirty, flushed on a timer or when evicted) | Immediately, synchronously with the cache write |
| write() latency | Fast — memory-speed | Slow — pays disk latency on every write |
| Crash risk | Dirty pages not yet flushed can be lost | Minimal — disk is always current |
| Typical use | Default OS page cache behavior (Linux, most OSes) | Databases and systems requiring strict durability guarantees on demand |

**How to decide:** write-back is the right default for general-purpose performance — most writes don't need instant durability. Systems that do (databases, anything promising a client "your data is saved") layer explicit `fsync()`/`fdatasync()` calls at the moments durability actually matters, rather than making every write synchronous.

slides.sectionTitle: Spooling: queuing output for a single-client device
slides.markdown:
**Spooling** (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) is buffering at a different scale: instead of smoothing byte-level speed mismatches, it queues entire jobs for a device that can only truly serve one client at a time — the canonical example is a shared printer. Multiple processes "print" by writing their output to a **spool directory** on disk; a single spooler process reads from that queue and sends jobs to the printer one at a time, in order.

This decouples the requesting processes (which return immediately once their job is spooled, not once it's actually printed) from the device's true one-at-a-time serialization — and it's exactly the model print queues, batch job systems, and even some email queuing systems still use today.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming a completed write() means data is safely on disk
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "`write()` returned success, so my data survives a crash from this point on."

**Why it's wrong:** as covered above, a normal `write()` only guarantees the data reached the page cache — it's visible to other reads on this machine, but it may sit as a dirty page for seconds before the kernel's background flusher writes it to disk. A crash, power loss, or kernel panic before that flush loses the data entirely, with `write()` having reported success the whole time.

**Correct model:** `write()`'s success means "accepted into the cache," not "durable." An application that needs a durability guarantee must call `fsync()` (all data + metadata) or `fdatasync()` (data only, usually faster) at the point it actually needs to know the bytes survived — this is exactly the gap [Journaling & Crash Consistency](journaling-and-crash-consistency) covers from the file-system side.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: how much the page cache actually saves
slides.markdown:
A page cache hit serves data at roughly RAM bandwidth — tens of gigabytes per second, sub-microsecond latency for a 4KB page. A cache miss on an HDD costs 1-10ms (a seek plus rotation); even a fast NVMe SSD miss costs tens to low hundreds of microseconds. The practical ratio: a warm cache hit can be 100-1000x faster than the equivalent disk read it avoided.

This is why database and web-server performance tuning so often comes down to "working set fits in the page cache or it doesn't" — a server with enough RAM to cache its entire hot dataset behaves completely differently (and far better) under load than one that's constantly missing to disk, even with identical CPU and disk hardware.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: O_DIRECT and bypassing the page cache on purpose
slides.markdown:
Sometimes the page cache actively hurts a workload — a database engine that implements its own, smarter caching (knowing exactly which pages are hot, unlike the OS's generic LRU-ish policy) doesn't want the OS double-buffering the same data and wasting RAM on a second, redundant copy. Linux's `O_DIRECT` flag on `open()` bypasses the page cache entirely, reading and writing straight to/from the application's own buffers.

A staff-level answer names the cost of this choice explicitly: `O_DIRECT` I/O has stricter alignment requirements (buffer size and offset must match the device's block size), loses the "free" read-ahead and write-behind the OS cache provides, and shifts *all* caching responsibility onto the application. Databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL/InnoDB use it deliberately, precisely because they've decided they can manage memory better than the generic OS cache for their specific access patterns — a genuine, hard-won engineering trade-off, not a default anyone should reach for casually.
